healthcareSystem: Extremely limited public healthcare system. Hospitals and clinics are severely under-resourced. Many healthcare facilities are run by NGOs and international organizations. Private clinics in Port-au-Prince offer marginally better care. The system has been devastated by natural disasters and political instability.
qualityNotes: Healthcare is critically limited. Port-au-Prince has a few private clinics that provide basic care, but even these lack reliable electricity, supplies, and specialist staff. Outside the capital, healthcare is virtually nonexistent. Medical evacuation to Miami, Santo Domingo, or elsewhere is essential for any serious condition. Security concerns complicate medical access.
pharmacyHours: Pharmacies in Port-au-Prince open roughly 8am-5pm weekdays. Hours are unreliable due to security concerns. Very few pharmacies outside the capital.
pharmacyTips: Bring ALL essential medications from home. Counterfeit and expired drugs are widespread. Only buy from the most reputable pharmacies if absolutely necessary. French and Haitian Creole are spoken. Stock is extremely unreliable. Do not rely on local supply for any critical medications.
prescriptionRules: Prescription enforcement is minimal. Medication availability is the primary barrier, not regulations. Drug quality is a serious concern.

restrictedMeds.name: Cannabis/CBD products
restrictedMeds.note: Illegal. Drug trafficking penalties are severe.

restrictedMeds.name: Narcotic painkillers
restrictedMeds.note: Carry a doctor's letter, original packaging, and be prepared for inspections.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications
restrictedMeds.note: Carry full documentation from your prescribing physician.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names, in French or English. Keep medications in original packaging. Bring your ENTIRE supply plus extra — medications are essentially unavailable locally. Consider bringing basic first-aid supplies as well.

travelInsurance.tips: Medical evacuation coverage is absolutely critical. Miami is the primary evacuation destination. Santo Domingo (Dominican Republic) is an alternative. Ensure your policy covers security-related evacuation as well as medical. Confirm your insurer operates in Haiti — some exclude it. Coverage for cholera and tropical diseases is essential.

required: Yellow Fever (only if arriving from a yellow fever endemic country)
recommended: Rabies (for extended stays or rural travel)
Malaria prophylaxis (malaria is present throughout Haiti)
vaccinations.notes: Cholera has been a significant health risk in Haiti. Malaria prophylaxis is recommended for all travelers. Mosquito-borne illnesses including dengue and Zika are also present. Bring a comprehensive medical kit.

waterNotes: Tap water is absolutely NOT safe to drink. Use only sealed bottled water or water purified with reliable filters/tablets for drinking, brushing teeth, and washing produce. Avoid all ice. Cholera is a risk from contaminated water. Carry your own water purification system.
foodSafetyTips: Eat only at well-established restaurants. Ensure all food is freshly cooked and served hot. Avoid raw vegetables, salads, and unpeeled fruit. Street food carries significant risk. Griot (fried pork) and diri ak djon djon (mushroom rice) from reputable restaurants are generally safe when fresh. Wash hands frequently.
medicalTourismNote: Haiti is not a medical tourism destination. The country has a severe healthcare crisis. For any non-emergency medical needs, travel to the Dominican Republic or the United States.
metaDescription: Haiti health guide. Emergency contacts, very limited healthcare, unsafe water, cholera and malaria risks, and critical evacuation info.

hospitals.name: Hôpital Bernard Mevs / Project Medishare
hospitals.notes: NGO-supported trauma and critical care hospital. One of the best-equipped facilities in Haiti. English and French spoken. Trauma center capability.

hospitals.name: Hôpital de l'Université d'État d'Haïti (HUEH)
hospitals.notes: Main government teaching hospital. Severely overcrowded and under-resourced. French/Creole speaking. Use only if no alternatives available.

hospitals.name: Hôpital Adventiste d'Haïti
hospitals.notes: Seventh-day Adventist hospital. Better maintained than public hospitals. English and French spoken. General and surgical care.

dentalCare.availability: Very limited. A few dental practices in Port-au-Prince. None in rural areas.
dentalCare.notes: Dental care is extremely basic. Some NGO-run dental clinics provide periodic services. Equipment and sterilization standards may not meet international norms.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: Pack a comprehensive dental emergency kit. For serious dental issues, evacuation to Santo Domingo or Miami is recommended.

mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Very few. Some NGO-supported counseling available in Port-au-Prince.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services are virtually nonexistent. Haiti has an extreme shortage of mental health professionals — fewer than a dozen psychiatrists for the entire country. Post-earthquake and ongoing crisis-related trauma is widespread. Some NGOs (Partners in Health, MSF) provide limited mental health support.

accessibilityInfo.overview: No accessibility infrastructure exists. Roads are severely damaged, sidewalks are broken or nonexistent, and buildings lack any accessibility features.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Hospitals are not wheelchair accessible. Building damage from earthquakes further limits access.
accessibilityInfo.transport: No accessible transport of any kind. Roads are in poor condition. Private vehicles with a driver are the only option.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Travel to Haiti with a disability is extremely challenging and generally not advised. A dedicated travel companion and local fixer are essential. Security concerns add further complexity.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements for entry as of 2026.
covidStatus.testing: Very limited COVID testing available at a few facilities in Port-au-Prince.
covidStatus.notes: COVID testing and treatment capacity is extremely limited. The healthcare system cannot handle surges of any respiratory illness.

insuranceClaimProcess: Keep all receipts and medical documentation. Cash payment is required at all facilities — credit cards are not widely accepted. Haitian gourde (HTG) and USD are both used. Submit claims with receipts to your insurer after returning home. Contact your insurer's emergency line immediately for any serious condition — they may coordinate direct evacuation.

commonCosts.note: Costs are low but quality is extremely poor. Cash only in most cases. USD is widely accepted alongside Haitian gourde. NGO-run facilities may provide care at reduced cost or free. Medical evacuation costs can exceed $30,000.

medicalEvacuation.note: Medical evacuation is the ONLY option for serious conditions. Port-au-Prince airport (Toussaint Louverture) is the departure point. Miami is about 90 minutes by air. Security conditions may complicate ground transport to the airport. Some insurers maintain evacuation coordinators in-country.
